findings.trigger: An admin pastes a Discord channel ID / user ID that carries a trailing newline (a common clipboard artifact) into a rule's channel_ids, allowed_user_ids, or notification_channel_id. DISCORD_SNOWFLAKE_PATTERN = re.compile(r'^\d{17,19}$') at line 26 is unanchored at the true end of the string: Python's `$` (without re.MULTILINE) also matches just before a trailing '\n'. So validate_discord_snowflake (line 68, .match at line 73) accepts e.g. '123456789012345678\n' as a valid snowflake. add_rule/update_rule then save it verbatim into auto_actions.json. At runtime, message.channel.id / message.author.id are compared as clean digit strings, which will never equal the stored value with its stray newline, so the rule silently never triggers - the panel reported 'created'/'updated' with no error anywhere.
findings.suggestion: Anchor the pattern with `\Z` instead of `$` (or use re.fullmatch with no `$`), and/or `.strip()` snowflake-like fields before validating and storing them.

findings.trigger: validate_rule_data reads both `keywords` (line 273) and `required_keywords` (line 274) from the trigger, but only `keywords` is checked against MAX_KEYWORDS=50 and MAX_KEYWORD_LENGTH=100 (lines 278-286). `required_keywords` and `ignore_keywords` (used identically at runtime per the TriggerConfig docstring - 'required_keywords: Must ALL match') are never checked for count or per-entry length, so a rule saved with e.g. 5,000 required_keywords, or single keywords far longer than 100 chars, passes validation unchanged - the two fields that do the same job (keyword matching) drifted apart.
findings.suggestion: Apply the same MAX_KEYWORDS / MAX_KEYWORD_LENGTH checks used for `keywords` to `required_keywords` and `ignore_keywords`.

findings.trigger: VALID_ACTION_TYPES = {'RESTART', 'STOP', 'START', 'RECREATE', 'NOTIFY'} (line 40) lets an admin save an auto-action rule with action.type='RECREATE' (checked at line 318). SPEC.md's Z6 guarantee states DDC exposes exactly three Docker actions (start/stop/restart) and says this was audited and pinned down specifically in docker_action_service.py:90-94 and docker_utils.py:626-631 - neither file is part of this review section, and nothing in the material given to me shows what code turns an AutoActionRule with action.type='RECREATE' into an actual Docker call.
findings.suggestion: Confirm, in the code that dispatches AutoActionRule.action.type to Docker (outside this section), that 'RECREATE' maps onto one of start/stop/restart and never calls remove()/kill()/prune(). If it does something else, that contradicts Z6 and needs the same audit treatment the other three actions got. Either way, a short comment near VALID_ACTION_TYPES pointing at that dispatch code would save the next reviewer this detour.
findings.unsure_why: The execution path that consumes action.type='RECREATE' (presumably in services/automation/automation_service.py or a docker action service) is not included in this section's source, so I cannot see whether it maps to a safe action or an actual container removal.

findings.trigger: services/automation/__init__.py (lines 6-8) eagerly imports auto_action_config_service, auto_action_state_service AND automation_service as soon as anything under services.automation is imported - including the lazy `from services.automation.automation_service import _resolved` inside this very section's validate_rule_data (auto_action_config_service.py:357), and any external `from services.automation.auto_action_config_service import get_auto_action_config_service`. This is the exact pattern services/__init__.py was rewritten to remove, per its own comment in this section's source: 'NOTHING IS IMPORTED HERE ON PURPOSE ... An ImportError anywhere in those five made services.config.config_service unimportable too.' Here, at the automation sub-package, that coupling still exists: an import-time failure in automation_service.py or auto_action_state_service.py would also break importing the unrelated auto_action_config_service.
findings.suggestion: Empty services/automation/__init__.py the same way services/__init__.py was emptied, and have callers import each concrete module directly.

findings.trigger: _save_config_file (lines 682-713) reimplements atomic writing instead of using utils/atomic_io.py. Unlike admin_service.py's _save_admin_data_unlocked (which does os.chmod(temp_path, stat.S_IMODE(admins_file.stat().st_mode)) before replacing), it never preserves the original file's permissions on the replacement. And on non-POSIX systems (line 702: `else:`) it does self.config_file.unlink() (line 703) and only then os.rename(...) (line 704) - exactly the 'opens a window with no file' pattern that SPEC.md's Z7 section names as the unsafe one of two pre-existing helpers and says utils/atomic_io.py was built to replace. This file is not among the five Z7 fixes SPEC.md lists, and still carries its own copy of that pattern.
findings.suggestion: Route _save_config_file through utils/atomic_io.py like the other five Z7 fixes, for consistency and permission preservation.
findings.unsure_why: n/a - noted low rather than higher severity because DDC's documented runtime is Linux/Alpine in Docker, where os.name == 'posix' and the risky unlink-then-rename branch is never executed; I cannot rule out some other consumer of this file caring about its permissions after a rewrite.

findings.trigger: get_current_language() (def at line 78) wraps `config = load_config()` (line 101) in `except Exception: return self._current_language or 'en'` (line 102) with no logging at all. This method sits behind `_()`, used for essentially every user-facing string. If load_config() starts throwing persistently (corrupt config.json, permissions, etc.), the bot silently and permanently falls back to the cached/English language with zero trace in the logs - nothing else in this file logs that branch being taken.
findings.suggestion: Log at least once (e.g. logger.warning, possibly rate-limited) when the except branch is taken, so a persistent load_config() failure is visible instead of only showing up as 'labels are in the wrong language'.

notes: Three smaller things I noticed but did not file as findings: (1) AutoActionConfigService.update_global_settings (line 857) rejects the WHOLE settings save with 'The alarm webhook must be an http(s) URL' unless valid_url(str(settings.get('alert_webhook_url') or '')) is true (line 867-869) - if valid_url('') returns False, every settings save that doesn't include a webhook URL would fail, but services/automation/alert_webhook.py (where valid_url lives) is not part of this section's source, so I could not confirm its behaviour on an empty string and did not want to guess. (2) validate_rule_data's `action_type = action.get('type', 'NOTIFY').upper()` (line 317) will raise AttributeError if the submitted rule_data has 'type' explicitly set to null (key present, value None - .get's default only applies when the key is absent). This is caught by the generic `except Exception` in add_rule/update_rule and turned into a raw Python error string instead of a clean validation message - a visible but ugly failure, not a silent one, so I left it out of the findings list. (3) AdminService.get_admin_data (admin_service.py:240) accepts a force_refresh parameter but never uses it - the method always reads admins.json straight from disk regardless of the flag, so the parameter is decorative rather than functional; harmless (it never returns stale data) but worth knowing if someone later assumes force_refresh=False is cheaper.
